accepted.question_text: Does every closed simply-connected 4-manifold admit a trisection in which one of the three 4-dimensional pieces is a 4-disk? Equivalently, is every closed simply-connected 4-manifold representable by a trisection having a 4-dimensional sector diffeomorphic to the 4-disk, rather than merely by a trisection in which all three sectors are higher-genus 4-dimensional handlebodies?

evidence.quote: As a consequence, only simply-connected 4-manifolds can admit trisections where one the 4-dimensional "pieces" is a 4-disk. Viceversa, it is an open problem whether each closed simply-connected 4-manifold admits a trisection with this property, or not

accepted.question_text: Can one develop an algorithmic procedure that converts generalized Kirby diagrams representing non-orientable 1-handles into gems of the corresponding 4-manifolds? In addition, do the resulting gems admit gem-induced trisections in enough generality that gem methods would then provide an estimation of trisection genus for all closed 4-manifolds, including the non-orientable setting?

evidence.quote: As regards Section 3.1, an interesting development would be to obtain an algorithmic procedure to pass from Kirby diagrams to gems in the generalized case of diagrams representing also non-orientable 1-handles (according to [19]).

If the resulting gems admitted gem-induced trisections (as happens in the orientable setting: see Theorem 17), in virtue of the non-orientable version of Laudenbach-Poenaru's result due to [32], an estimation of the trisection genus for all closed 4-manifolds would be obtained, via gems.

accepted.question_text: Suppose one starts with a gem of the compact 4-manifold consisting only of the handles of index at most two. Can one construct from it a gem of the associated closed 4-manifold even when the original gem contains no rho3-pair and no rho4-pair? More specifically, can one recognize or create the combinatorial structures needed to pass from the bounded handlebody stage to the closed manifold stage without assuming the special pair configurations used in Proposition 9?
accepted.context_brief: closing gems without rho3 or rho4 pairs

evidence.quote: Another possible improvement would be to study how to obtain a gem of a closed 4-manifold, starting from a gem of the compact one consisting only of handles up to index two, even if no ρ3- or ρ4-pair appears in the latter (as assumed in Proposition 9).

The problem is obviously a difficult one, since it involves the combinatorial recognition of #m(S1 x S2) (m > 0) in 3-dimensional topology, but in specific situations it could possibly be faced, for example by detecting sequences of combinatorial moves yielding the desired ρ3-pairs.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a compact 4-manifold, and form the double of M by taking a Kirby diagram of M and adding a 0-framed meridian to each framed component, which yields a Kirby diagram of the double. For the resulting 5-colored graph produced by the paper's construction, can one modify that graph in a standard way so as to create rho3-pairs satisfying the hypotheses of Proposition 9, thereby giving a direct gem-theoretic route to the double?

evidence.quote: A particular case of this problem arises, for instance, in the construction of a gem for the double of a compact 4-manifold. It is known that a Kirby diagram of the double can be obtained, from a Kirby diagram of the manifold itself, by adding a 0-framed meridian to each framed component (see [24]).

Therefore, it may be worth investigating whether the particular configuration of the arising 5-colored graph allows to be modified in a standard way so as to give rise to ρ3-pairs satisfying Proposition 9.

accepted.question_text: Can one characterize classes of gems for which the trisections arising from those gems actually realize the trisection genus of the represented 4-manifolds? In other words, beyond merely producing or bounding trisections from gems, which combinatorial or topological conditions on a gem guarantee that the trisection obtained from it has minimum possible genus for the underlying 4-manifold?

evidence.quote: With respect to Section 3.2, a fundamental problem involves the possible characterization of classes of gems so that the arising trisections (either directly, as gem-induced trisections, or indirectly, via the approach described in Section 3.2.2) realize the trisection genus of the represented 4-manifolds.

accepted.question_text: Which closed simply-connected 4-manifolds admit a 5-colored graph Γ in G_s^(4) and a cyclic permutation ε of the color set such that g_{ε0,ε2,ε4} = 1 and g_{ε1,ε3,ε4} = 1 and the associated T(Γ, ε) is a gem-induced trisection, so that the trisection genus equals the second Betti number β2(M)? More generally, can one characterize topologically the 4-manifolds that admit gems satisfying the hypotheses used in Proposition 26, or at least identify broad classes of manifolds that do so?

evidence.quote: Proposition 26 ([10]) gT(M) = β2(M) for each closed (simply-connected) 4-manifold M which admits a 5-colored graph Γ ∈ G^(4)_s representing M with gε0,ε2,ε4 = 1 and gε1,ε3,ε4 = 1 (ε being a cyclic permutation of ∆4), so that T(Γ, ε) is a gem-induced trisection.
It would be very interesting to characterize topologically 4-manifolds admitting gems which satisfy the hypotheses of the above statement, or at least to find classes satisfying them.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a compact 4-manifold with boundary homeomorphic to a connected sum #m(S1 ⊗ S2), with m > 0, and let Mbar be the associated closed 4-manifold obtained by attaching the corresponding 4-dimensional handlebody. Theorem 13 states that if M admits a gem-induced trisection, then Mbar admits a trisection with the same central surface and therefore gT(Mbar) <= gGT(M). Under what conditions on a gem of M does equality hold, so that the trisection genus of Mbar is exactly the G-trisection genus of M?

evidence.quote: Theorem 13 ([11]) Let M be a compact 4-manifold with boundary ∂M ∼= #m(S1 ⊗S2), with m > 0. If M admits a gem-induced trisection, then Mbar ∼= M ∪ Y^(~)_m admits a trisection with the same central surface. As a consequence, gT(Mbar) ≤ gGT(M).
On the other hand, it would also be interesting to investigate conditions on the gems of a compact 4-manifold, so that in Theorem 13 the equality holds.
